title: Death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade (4.4)
hook: a small creature at the end of a blade of grass never lets go until it has hold of the next one
tomorrow: "as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed"

segments.voice: Yesterday, deep sleep: the falcon folding its wings, held by the knowing self, with no inside and no outside. Did the day's names go one by one as you fell asleep? Day three hundred eighty-five.

Crouch down in a garden and watch a caterpillar climb a blade of grass. When it reaches the tip, it doesn't fall off, and it doesn't jump. It stretches its front end out into the air, waving a little, until it touches the next blade. It grips. Only then does it let go of the old one and draw the rest of itself across. Yajnavalkya and King Janaka have walked through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Now the king's teacher takes the last step, the one everyone takes, and he uses that caterpillar.
screen: `AT THE TIP OF A BLADE OF GRASS.` → `IT REACHES, AND GRIPS.` → `ONLY THEN DOES IT LET GO.`

segments.voice: First he describes the dying, gently and closely. The person grows weak and seems confused. The senses gather around the self, the way a king's officers gather when he's about to travel. The self draws all its powers in and goes down into the heart. People around the bed say: he doesn't see now, he doesn't hear now. He's becoming one. Then the tip of the heart lights up, and by that light the self leaves, and the breath and the senses follow. And what goes with it? What it knew, and what it did, and what it had lived. Then the picture. As a caterpillar, coming to the end of a blade of grass, reaches out to another and draws itself across, so the self, having laid down this body and let go of not-knowing, reaches out to another support and draws itself across. And one more: as a goldsmith takes a piece of gold and hammers it into another shape, newer and more beautiful, so the self makes itself another form. Notice what these pictures say. There's no gap in the caterpillar's crossing: it doesn't let go into nothing. And the gold is the same gold. You met Krishna's picture in the Gita last year, old clothes laid aside for new ones; it belongs to the same family. Look back at this week. Gargi's two arrows. The gods counted down to one. Shakalya's head. The light of the self. The dreamer building. Deep sleep's embrace. And today, the leaf.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER; THE HEART LIGHTS UP.` · `WHAT IT KNEW, DID, AND LIVED GOES WITH IT.` · `THE CATERPILLAR REACHES THE NEXT BLADE.` · `THE GOLDSMITH'S GOLD, NEWLY SHAPED.` · then, large: `THE LEAF.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of reaching and letting go. Sit, and breathe. At the very end of each out-breath, notice the tiny reach toward the next breath, before the old one is quite finished. Then let the old breath go. Don't hurry it. If thoughts about death come, someone you've lost, or your own, let them be here too, and keep breathing through them, one blade to the next. The bell holds the time.
Death, as the Brihadaranyaka pictures it: a caterpillar at the tip of a blade of grass, reaching for the next before it lets go.
Your line: the leaf. Today, when you finish something, notice whether you've already reached for the next thing before you let go. Day three hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 385 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "AS IS HIS DESIRE, SO IS HIS WILL."`

howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, are performed by the family with fire and mantras, and the days that follow include offerings for the departed; passages like this one and Bhagavad Gita 2.22 may be read or recalled at the time of a death.

fork.setup: you're a caterpillar at the very tip of a blade of grass. what do you do?
options: reach out, grip the next blade, then draw yourself across.
fork.reveal: it reaches, grips, and only then lets go. so, the text says, the self lays down this body and draws itself across to another support.

original.note: Sanskrit tṛṇa (grass) + jalāyukā: a creature that moves blade to blade; translators say caterpillar or leech.

trapdoor: what you thought: death is a fall into nothing.
what it means: in this picture, the self reaches the next support before it lets go, carrying what it knew and did.
what a scholar hears: 4.4.3's tṛṇajalāyukā is rendered caterpillar or leech; 4.4.4's goldsmith and Gita 2.22's clothes are kindred images of rebirth.

notes: The index word is 'Death' (the title's head); kept exactly.
The king's-officers simile for the gathering senses is from the end of 4.3 (4.3.37–38); the dying description (4.4.1–2) is paraphrased. Confirm.
Knowledge, deeds and past experience (vidyā-karmaṇī pūrvaprajñā ca, 4.4.2): confirm the rendering.
Tṛṇajalāyukā: translated caterpillar (Hume, Olivelle) or leech; confirm.
Death is a sensitive subject; the practice invites but does not require thinking about a loss.
